Under water, without oxygen, rot fungi and insects cannot live. If the groundwater table drops, the pile heads come into the air and start to rot.

An auger of a few flights at the end of the Kelly bar. It drills down, fills up, the rig lifts it out, then spins the soil off beside the bore – and starts again. It is effective mainly in cohesive soil: granular soil trickles out from between the flights.

The auger runs along the whole pile length and penetrates to the final depth in a single pass. The spoil stays between the flights and supports the wall of the bore meanwhile – this is the basis of the CFA pile. It can be used in any soil.

Cylindrical grab: it is dropped to the bottom of the bore with open jaws, bites into the soil as it closes, and is emptied beside the bore. It can be used in any soil, in fill and stony layers too; it often works under the protection of a steel casing.

A cylindrical bucket with a toothed bottom: while it rotates, the soil enters the bucket through the opening in its bottom. When full it is lifted out and emptied through the hinged bottom flap. Effective mainly in granular soil, where the soil would trickle off an auger.

The drilling head only breaks up and loosens the soil at the bottom of the bore; the loosened material is carried out by the flushing fluid: down the drill rod, up the gap between the rod and the wall of the bore, and into a settling tank at the surface. Common for small-diameter drilling and micropiles.

If the excavation gets ahead of the casing, in granular soil the free wall section below the casing collapses, the soil flows into the bore under the casing, and the surroundings loosen. In granular soil the casing must always go ahead of the excavation.

The water inside the casing is ${fmt(-dh, 1)} m lower than outside. The difference starts an upward flow at the base: the water breaks in, carries grains with it, and loosens the soil where the pile base will sit. The water removed must be replaced.

In fine sand below the groundwater, CFA needs particular care (it is not even recommended in loose, flowing soil): if the auger rotates too much relative to its penetration, it brings up more soil than the volume of the bore, and the surroundings loosen.
